note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: Is the byte passed as an integer or as a binary string?
Is the returned byte an integer?
Must the MSB be cleared when the low bits already have even parity?
hints: Only bit 7 is free; bits 0 to 6 are fixed.
The MSB must equal the parity of the seven low bits.
Fold the low bits with XOR shifts until bit 0 holds their parity.
invariants: result & 127 == byte & 127
popcount(result) is even
chooseWhen: A parity bit must be set on fixed-width data with bit operations only
tradeoffs: A lookup table of 128 entries is equally fast but hides the reasoning

clarifyingQuestions: Is the objective the longest single day?
May fewer than k rests be used?
Can two stops share a distance?
hints: Using more rests never makes the longest day longer, so feasibility is monotone in D.
For a fixed D, walking as far as possible each day uses the fewest days.
Binary search D between the largest adjacent gap and t[n-1]; D is feasible when the greedy walk needs at most k + 1 days.
invariants: the answer is at least max(t[i+1] - t[i])
the answer is at most t[n-1]
chooseWhen: A min-max partition of a line into a bounded number of pieces
tradeoffs: A DP is exact for any objective but quadratic; the binary search needs monotone feasibility

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when source equals target?
Can edges repeat or be self-loops?
Is the graph connected?
hints: Every edge has the same length, so breadth-first order is distance order.
Build adjacency lists once from the edge list.
Stop as soon as target is reached; return -1 when the queue empties first.
invariants: nodes are dequeued in non-decreasing distance
each node is enqueued at most once
chooseWhen: All edges have equal weight
tradeoffs: Dijkstra also works but adds a heap for no benefit

clarifyingQuestions: What does move return?
Does the tail cell count as occupied on a non-growing move?
What happens to moves after the game ends?
Is growth on the fifth move or after it?
hints: The head and tail change at opposite ends: a deque fits.
Keep a set of occupied cells next to the deque so self-collision is a hash lookup.
On a non-growing move remove the tail from both structures before testing the new head cell.
invariants: the deque and the set hold the same cells
length = 1 + floor(moves / 5) while the game runs
chooseWhen: A body moves by adding at one end and removing at the other
tradeoffs: A grid of booleans gives O(1) lookups but costs rows * cols memory
hack2hire:68c48c55e558bc07a7541e31.variantLabel: Inferred: boolean move, growth on every fifth move

constraints: timestamps are valid dates in years 1970 to 2099
clarifyingQuestions: Does one call matched by two reports count twice?
Are callers with zero matches listed?
How is the output ordered?
Can timestamps cross a day or year boundary?
hints: Group report times by receiver and sort each group.
For one call, the matching reports are a contiguous range of its receiver's sorted times.
Two binary searches give the range size; add it to the caller's total.
invariants: each reported count equals the number of matching (call, report) pairs of that caller
output counts are positive
chooseWhen: Many calls and reports share a receiver and windows overlap
tradeoffs: Pair enumeration is simpler but quadratic per receiver
hack2hire:6842720b61bdd61d17676953.variantLabel: Inferred: per-caller count of matching pairs

clarifyingQuestions: In what order are words returned?
Are repeated dictionary words returned twice?
May optionalLetters contain the required letter?
hints: Precompute the allowed letters as a set or bit mask.
A word is valid when its letters are a subset of the allowed set and include the required letter.
Check the length first; it is the cheapest rule.
invariants: returned words form a subsequence of dictionary
chooseWhen: A small fixed alphabet makes bit masks natural
tradeoffs: Sets are clearer; masks avoid allocation per word

clarifyingQuestions: Are overlapping occurrences replaced?
Can target be empty?
Can replacement be empty?
hints: Scan left to right; after a match, continue right after it so matches never overlap.
A naive comparison at every position is quadratic on inputs like "aaaa...".
KMP finds each match in linear time; reset the state to 0 after a match to forbid overlap.
invariants: matches are disjoint and each is the leftmost one starting after the previous match
chooseWhen: Built-in search is unavailable and inputs may be adversarial
tradeoffs: A naive scan is simpler and often fast, but quadratic in the worst case

clarifyingQuestions: What is the input day budget called and what is returned when it is too small?
Can a day span two chapters?
Is x an integer?
hints: A day never spans two chapters, so chapter i alone needs ceil(pages[i] / x) days.
The total day count only falls as x grows.
Binary search x between 1 and max(pages); at x = max(pages) the count is n.
invariants: days(x) is non-increasing in x
days(max(pages)) = n
chooseWhen: The answer is the smallest parameter that satisfies a monotone budget
tradeoffs: A linear scan over x is simple but far too slow at large page counts
hack2hire:67801e4c6fee41e51af73dda.variantLabel: Inferred: smallest daily limit within a day budget

constraints: author test cap: min(k, sum(nums) - k) <= 10^6 whenever k < sum(nums)
clarifyingQuestions: Can one position be used twice?
Do equal values at different positions count as different elements?
How large can k be in practice?
hints: A subset sums to k exactly when its complement sums to sum - k, so work with the smaller target.
Track every reachable sum up to the target as bits of one integer.
Adding value x maps the bit set B to B | (B << x); stop as soon as the target bit is set.
invariants: bit s is set iff some subset of the processed prefix sums to s
chooseWhen: Targets are moderate and only feasibility is needed
tradeoffs: Memoised search is closer to the tags but can revisit exponentially many (index, remainder) states

constraints: author test cap: n * min(k, sum(nums) - k) <= 10^6 whenever k < sum(nums)
clarifyingQuestions: Are subsets with equal values at different positions different?
Is the count reduced modulo a prime?
Is the empty subset ever counted (k >= 1)?
hints: Count subsets reaching each sum, not just whether it is reachable.
Process elements one at a time; go through sums from high to low so each element is used once.
Counting subsets with sum k equals counting complements with sum S - k; use the smaller target and reduce modulo 1000000007.
invariants: ways[s] counts subsets of the processed prefix with sum s, modulo 1000000007
chooseWhen: A number of subsets is wanted and the target is moderate
tradeoffs: Exact big counts would need big integers; the modulus keeps values below 2^31

constraints: author test cap: at most 10000 combinations
clarifyingQuestions: Are combinations deduplicated by value?
What order is required inside and across combinations?
May a value be reused beyond its multiplicity?
hints: Group equal values; a combination is a choice of how many copies of each distinct value.
Plain backtracking can wander through huge dead-end regions; first compute which sums each suffix of distinct values can make.
Enumerate values in ascending order, taking 0..multiplicity copies, and enter a branch only when the remainder is reachable from the next suffix; this yields lexicographic order directly.
invariants: every emitted combination sums to k
the enumeration never enters a branch with no completion
chooseWhen: All solutions must be listed and dead ends are common
tradeoffs: The reachability table costs O(D * k) bits but makes the enumeration output-sensitive

clarifyingQuestions: Is "first" the leftmost start or the first element in list order?
If several elements start at the same position, which wins?
Is more than one substring per word wrapped?
hints: Handle each word separately; at most one wrap per word.
Scanning start positions left to right finds the leftmost match first.
A trie lets one walk from a start position report every element beginning there; keep the deepest terminal.
invariants: each output word without its brackets equals the input word
each output word has at most one bracket pair
chooseWhen: Many patterns must be found at the same start positions
tradeoffs: Checking every element at every position is simpler but multiplies by the element count

clarifyingQuestions: Can a value contain braces?
Are keys distinct?
Can placeholders be adjacent?
hints: Build a map from name to value.
Scan once: copy ordinary characters; at "{" read up to the matching "}".
Collect pieces in a list and join once at the end.
invariants: output = text with each {name} replaced by map[name]
chooseWhen: Placeholders are flat and well formed
tradeoffs: A regex is shorter; the manual scan makes the linear cost explicit

clarifyingQuestions: Can values refer to other keys?
Can references form a cycle?
Is the expansion of a key reused when it appears many times?
hints: A value with placeholders must be expanded before it is substituted.
Expand each key once and cache it; reuse the cache for every later reference.
Chains of references can be long, so replace recursion with an explicit stack processed in dependency order.
invariants: a cached expansion contains no braces
each key is expanded once
chooseWhen: Values reference each other and appear many times
tradeoffs: Caching expansions can store long strings; recomputation would repeat work exponentially in the worst case

constraints: block is 1..10 x 1..10 with at least one 1
the landed block lies fully inside the grid (inferred precondition)
clarifyingQuestions: Where does the block start?
What is returned: the grid or the landing row?
What if the block cannot fully enter the grid?
hints: The block falls from above, so in each column its lowest 1-cell meets any obstacle first.
In each grid column under the block, only the highest occupied cell (or the floor) matters.
The landing shift is the minimum over block columns of (first obstacle row - 1 - lowest block row in that column).
invariants: landed block cells never overlap background 1s
one more row down would collide or leave the grid
chooseWhen: A rigid shape falls without rotation onto a static grid
tradeoffs: Simulation is easy to trust; the column profile is linear in the grid
hack2hire:6aa861838c97c56cdbdc93e2.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: place the landed block

constraints: block is 1..10 x 1..10 with at least one 1
the landed block lies fully inside the grid (inferred precondition)
clarifyingQuestions: Are rows that were already full before the drop also cleared?
Do cleared rows cascade further?
Does the grid keep its height?
hints: Land the block exactly as in level 1.
A row is cleared when every cell is 1; clearing only shifts rows down, so no new row becomes full.
Copy non-full rows bottom-up into a fresh grid and fill the top with zero rows.
invariants: the output has the same shape as background
no output row is full
chooseWhen: The Tetris clearing rule follows a placement
tradeoffs: One compaction pass avoids repeated row deletions

constraints: each pair names two different listed nodes; repeats allowed
clarifyingQuestions: Are adjacencies given by name or index?
Can a node be adjacent to itself?
Do nodes without edges matter?
hints: Map names to indices and build adjacency lists.
Colour the node with the fewest remaining colours first; dead ends show up early.
Colour components independently and fix the first node's colour to break symmetry.
invariants: no two adjacent coloured nodes share a colour at any point of the search
chooseWhen: Small graphs with an NP-hard decision
tradeoffs: Exhaustive search is simplest; DSATUR ordering prunes most branches in practice

constraints: player in {1, 2}; moves on empty cells; no move after a win
clarifyingQuestions: What does move return?
Do longer runs than k also win?
Are both diagonal directions counted?
hints: Only lines through the newest mark can become winning.
Count consecutive own marks in both directions along each of the four lines through the new cell.
A sparse map of occupied cells keeps memory proportional to the moves, not the board.

chooseWhen: Large boards with few moves and arbitrary k
tradeoffs: Row/column counters (LeetCode 348) only work when k equals the line length

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned for a degenerate triangle?
Is a point on an edge inside?
What codes are returned for the four membership cases?
hints: Collinearity of a, b, c is a zero cross product.
A point is in the closed triangle when it is never strictly on opposite sides of two edges.
Integer cross products are exact; keep coordinates small enough that products stay below 2^53.

constraints: per user: departure < arrival <= next departure
clarifyingQuestions: What is returned while the user is in the air?
Where is the user before the first flight?
Which airport wins at an exact departure or arrival time?
What is returned for an unknown user?
hints: Only the queried user's flights matter.
Fixed-width ISO times compare correctly as strings.
Sort by departure time and binary search the last flight that departed at or before the query; then compare with its arrival time.
